subjects.name: Geschichte
subjects.description: Usually starts in Kl. 6 (sometimes Kl. 5 or 7) and runs to the Abitur. Kl. 5/6 cover method, prehistory and antiquity; Kl. 7–10 form a chronological course from the High Middle Ages to reunification in 1990, with National Socialism and the Holocaust at its centre. The Oberstufe adds source criticism, history culture and remembrance, and thematic deepening (nation, modernity, democracy and dictatorship, Europe and global history), following the KMK EPA Geschichte.

subjects.name: Erdkunde
subjects.description: Called Erdkunde (NRW, Niedersachsen), Geographie (Bayern, BW) or Geografie (Berlin/Brandenburg). After map skills and Germany and Europe in Kl. 5/6, Kl. 7–10 cover the Earth as a whole: plate tectonics and natural hazards, climate and landscape zones, water, land use, population and migration, cities, development and globalisation, and climate change. The Oberstufe adds regional analysis, urban and economic geography, sustainable development, resources and energy, and global disparities, following the KMK EPA Geographie.

subjects.name: Politik und Wirtschaft
subjects.description: Civic and economic education under many names: Wirtschaft-Politik (NRW), Politik-Wirtschaft (Niedersachsen), Politik und Gesellschaft plus Wirtschaft und Recht (Bayern), Gemeinschaftskunde and Wirtschaft (BW), Politische Bildung (Berlin/Brandenburg), Sozialkunde (several Länder); in the Oberstufe often Sozialwissenschaften (NRW) or Politik und Wirtschaft (Hessen). It starts with family, school and municipality in Kl. 5/6 and covers the Grundgesetz, democracy, the rule of law, the EU, the social market economy, consumer and career education and international politics in Kl. 7–10. The Oberstufe adds political theory, sociology, economic policy, globalisation and peace and security policy, following the KMK EPA Sozialkunde/Politik and Wirtschaft.

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Interpreting a Written Source
topics.description: Pupils work through a written source in fixed steps: describe it formally (author, date, addressee, type), summarise its content, place it in its historical context and judge its perspective and reliability.
evidence: Identifies author, date, addressee and type of a source before reading for content
Explains what the author wanted to achieve and from which position he or she wrote
Uses context knowledge to say what the source reveals and what it leaves out
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were given a short letter written by a medieval townsman, could they say who wrote it, why, and how far we can trust it?

prerequisites.reason: Interpretation presupposes knowing what a source is
Builds on the types of sources met in Kl. 6
Reading strategies for factual texts are reused

osMatches.note: os asks who/when/why; no full interpretation scheme

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Analysing Pictures and Cartoons
topics.description: Pupils analyse paintings, photographs, posters and political cartoons as historical sources: they describe the image, decode symbols and allegories, and explain the message and intended effect in context.
evidence: Describes an image systematically before interpreting it
Decodes symbols, allegories and exaggerations in a political cartoon
Explains the cartoonist's or photographer's intention against the historical context
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a 19th-century cartoon of Bismarck, could they decode its symbols and explain what the cartoonist wanted to say?

prerequisites.reason: Uses the same steps of source interpretation
Pictures were introduced as a source type in Kl. 6

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Factual and Value Judgements
topics.description: Pupils distinguish a factual judgement (how did it happen and why, judged by the standards of the time) from a value judgement (how do we assess it by today's values) and support both with evidence.
evidence: Sorts statements about a historical event into factual and value judgements
Judges an action by the standards and options of its own time
Writes a value judgement that names the present-day value it applies
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether Luther was right to oppose the peasants, could they separate a judgement from the 1525 viewpoint from one based on today's values?

prerequisites.reason: Giving reasons for a judgement is practised in Ethik
Judgements rest on sources and accounts

osMatches.note: os: judging people by the standards of their own time

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Multiple Perspectives in History
topics.description: Pupils compare how different contemporaries saw the same event (e.g. revolutionaries, nobles, peasants) and how later historians interpret it differently, and learn that history is told from perspectives.
evidence: Compares two contemporary sources on the same event and explains the differences
Explains how social position, interests or nationality shape a perspective
Distinguishes perspectives in the sources from controversies among historians
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read a French and a German account of the 1870 war, could they explain why the two tell such different stories?

prerequisites.reason: Comparing perspectives requires interpreting each source
Distinguishes contemporary views from later accounts

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: History in Films, Games and Museums
topics.nameDe: Geschichte in Film, Spiel und Museum untersuchen
topics.description: Pupils analyse historical accounts in school books, documentaries, feature films, computer games and museums, asking what is fact, what is interpretation or invention, and why history is presented this way.
evidence: Separates documented facts from fictional elements in a historical film or game
Explains how a museum or exhibition selects and arranges the past
Judges how far a popular account is plausible against sources
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} played a computer game set in the Thirty Years' War, could they point out what is historically plausible and what is invented for entertainment?

prerequisites.reason: History in media are accounts, not sources
Continues the primary-school look at history in media

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Memorials and Places of Remembrance
topics.description: Pupils examine how societies remember: war memorials, concentration camp memorial sites, Stolpersteine and days of remembrance (27 January, 9 November), and ask who is remembered, how and why.
evidence: Describes a local memorial and explains whom it commemorates and when it was built
Explains the purpose of a concentration-camp memorial site and of Stolpersteine
Compares how a monument from 1920 and one from today remember war
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} passed a Stolperstein on the pavement, could they explain what it is, whom it remembers and why it was set there?

prerequisites.reason: Days of remembrance were met in primary school
Memorials are another form of history culture

topics.laenderNotes: Visits to concentration-camp memorial sites are part of history teaching in many Länder, usually in Kl. 9/10 (in Bayern e.g. Dachau or Flossenbürg).

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Emperor and Pope
topics.nameDe: Kaiser und Papst: Reichskirche und Investiturstreit
topics.description: Pupils explain how the Ottonian and Salian kings ruled with the help of bishops (Reichskirche) and why this led to the Investiture Controversy with the papacy (Canossa 1077, Concordat of Worms 1122).
evidence: Explains why kings appointed bishops and abbots
Describes the conflict between Henry IV and Gregory VII and the walk to Canossa
Explains the compromise of the Concordat of Worms
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard someone say "We are not going to Canossa", could they explain the medieval conflict behind the phrase?

prerequisites.reason: Continues Frankish rule and the imperial idea
The church as an institution goes back to late antiquity

osMatches.note: os: power of the medieval Church, no Investiture Controversy

topics.laenderNotes: Central in Bayern (Kl. 7, LB 1) and BW; NRW's Kernlehrplan G9 does not name the Investiture Controversy explicitly.

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Feudalism and Territorial Princes
topics.description: Building on the feudal pyramid of Kl. 6, pupils explain how hereditary fiefs, an elected kingship and the Golden Bull (1356) let princes build their own territories, so that the Holy Roman Empire stayed decentralised.
evidence: Explains how fiefs became hereditary and what that meant for royal power
Names the prince-electors and the role of the Golden Bull
Explains why Germany remained a patchwork of territories unlike France or England
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared a map of the Holy Roman Empire around 1400 with a map of France, could they explain why the Empire looks like a patchwork?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on the feudal pyramid introduced in Kl. 6
The struggle with the papacy weakened royal power

osMatches.note: os: limiting royal power in England

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Life in the Medieval Town
topics.nameDe: Die mittelalterliche Stadt: Gründung und Stadtgesellschaft
topics.description: Pupils explain why lords founded towns (markets, tolls, protection), how town law and self-government developed, and describe town society from patricians and guilds to the poor ("Stadtluft macht frei").
evidence: Explains the interests of a town founder using a regional example
Describes the roles of council, guilds and burghers in a medieval town
Discusses why life in a town was attractive to peasants
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} walked through an old town centre with a market square, town hall and guild houses, could they explain how the medieval town was organised?

prerequisites.reason: Town freedom is defined against manorial dependence
Monasteries and castles were the earlier centres of medieval life

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Jewish Life in Medieval Towns
topics.nameDe: Jüdisches Leben im Mittelalter und Pestpogrome
topics.description: Pupils describe Jewish communities in medieval towns (e.g. the SchUM cities Speyer, Worms and Mainz), their legal position under royal protection, and the persecutions during the crusades and the Black Death (1348–50).
evidence: Describes the legal position and everyday life of a Jewish community
Explains how the Black Death spread and how Jews were blamed for it
Assesses the change between coexistence and persecution
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visited the Jewish quarter of Worms, could they explain how Jews lived there in the Middle Ages and why the community suffered pogroms?

prerequisites.reason: Jewish communities lived within the medieval town
Basic knowledge of Judaism from Religion/Ethik

osMatches.note: os: Black Death without the pogroms

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Crusades
topics.description: Pupils explain the call to the First Crusade (1095), the motives of the crusaders, the conquest of Jerusalem and its consequences, and judge the crusades between conflict and cultural exchange among Christians, Muslims and Jews.
evidence: Names religious, economic and political motives of crusaders
Compares Christian and Muslim accounts of the conquest of Jerusalem
Judges the crusades with regard to coexistence and conflict
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read a Christian and an Arab report about the capture of Jerusalem in 1099, could they explain why the accounts differ so much?

prerequisites.reason: The crusades presuppose the spread of Islam
The papacy's claim to leadership explains the call to crusade

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Medieval Long-Distance Trade
topics.nameDe: Fernhandel im Mittelalter: Hanse, Seidenstraße, Transsahara
topics.description: Pupils describe medieval trade networks linking Europe, Asia and Africa – the Hanseatic League, the Silk Road and the trans-Saharan trade – and compare a European with an African trading city such as Lübeck or Venice and Timbuktu.
evidence: Locates the main routes and goods of Hanseatic, Silk Road and trans-Saharan trade
Compares a European and an African trading metropolis
Explains how trade spread knowledge and cultural contact
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a map of medieval trade routes, could they explain what was traded between Europe, Asia and Africa and why Timbuktu became rich?

prerequisites.reason: Trading cities and merchant guilds grew within towns
Earlier trade networks were met in Kl. 6

osMatches.note: os: Silk Road, Mali and the Islamic world

topics.laenderNotes: NRW requires transcontinental trade incl. Africa; Bayern lets teachers choose between the Hanse and early capitalism (Fugger).

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Renaissance, Humanism and Printing
topics.description: Pupils describe the new view of humans and nature in Renaissance and Humanism (e.g. Leonardo, Erasmus, Copernicus) and judge how Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1450) changed communication and society.
evidence: Explains what was "reborn" in the Renaissance and how the view of humans changed
Gives examples of changes in art and science from the Middle Ages to the early modern period
Judges the effects of the printing press on knowledge and religion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared a medieval painting with one by Leonardo or Dürer, could they explain what changed in how people saw the world?

prerequisites.reason: Wealthy towns were the centres of the Renaissance
Placing the turn from Middle Ages to early modern period

osMatches.note: os focuses on Caxton and England

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Voyages of Discovery and Conquest
topics.description: Pupils explain the preconditions, motives and course of the European voyages (Columbus 1492, da Gama) and the conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires, and assess the consequences for the indigenous peoples (violence, disease, Columbian exchange).
evidence: Names technical and economic preconditions of the voyages
Describes the conquest of the Aztec empire from European and indigenous perspectives
Assesses the consequences of the conquest for the Americas and Europe
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that Columbus "discovered" America, could they explain why historians question this word and what the conquest meant for the people living there?

prerequisites.reason: New knowledge and maps made the voyages possible
The search for new trade routes to Asia motivated the voyages

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Early Capitalism and Global Trade
topics.description: Pupils explain how merchant houses like the Fugger of Augsburg earned money through trade, mining and loans, how money financed politics (election of Charles V in 1519), and how trade routes shifted to the Atlantic.
evidence: Describes the business fields of the Fugger
Explains how Jakob Fugger's loans influenced the imperial election of 1519
Explains why trade routes shifted from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visited the Fuggerei in Augsburg, could they explain how the Fugger became so rich and why emperors depended on them?

prerequisites.reason: Early capitalism grew out of medieval long-distance trade
Understanding money and credit

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Luther and the Reformation
topics.description: Pupils explain the criticism of the church (indulgences), Luther's theses (1517) and the Diet of Worms (1521), the Peasants' War (1525) and the Peace of Augsburg (1555), and judge Luther's intentions against the intended and unintended results.
evidence: Explains why Luther attacked the sale of indulgences
Explains the role of the printing press and the princes in spreading the Reformation
Judges Luther's stance in the Peasants' War and the principle "cuius regio, eius religio"
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why there are both Protestant and Catholic regions in Germany today, could they trace this back to the Reformation and 1555?

prerequisites.reason: Printing and Humanism made the Reformation possible
Earlier conflicts over church power

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Witch Hunts
topics.description: Pupils explain the causes and motives of the witch hunts of the 16th and 17th centuries (crises, fears, beliefs, denunciation, trial procedures with torture) using a regional example.
evidence: Describes the course of a witch trial with a regional example
Explains why mainly women were accused
Explains how crises and beliefs made persecution possible
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read the record of a 1620s witch trial from their region, could they explain why the accused had almost no chance?

prerequisites.reason: Confessional conflicts and fears shaped the period
Trial records are interpreted as sources

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Thirty Years' War
topics.nameDe: Der Dreißigjährige Krieg und der Westfälische Frieden
topics.description: Pupils explain the religious and political causes of the Thirty Years' War (1618–48), its consequences for the population (violence, hunger, plague, depopulation) and the results of the Peace of Westphalia.
evidence: Explains religious and power-political causes of the war
Describes the war's impact on civilians using sources
Names results of the Peace of Westphalia for the Empire and Europe
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a population chart showing a German region losing a third of its people between 1618 and 1648, could they explain why?

prerequisites.reason: The confessional split is a cause of the war
The territorial princes were key actors

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Absolutism: Louis XIV
topics.description: Pupils explain absolute monarchy using Louis XIV: divine right, court society at Versailles, standing army, bureaucracy and mercantilism, and compare it with a German example (e.g. Prussia or a Bavarian or Württemberg residence).
evidence: Explains the pillars of absolutist rule
Explains the idea and aims of mercantilism
Analyses a baroque palace as an expression of political power
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} toured a baroque palace like the Würzburg Residenz, could they explain how its design showed the ruler's power?

prerequisites.reason: Absolutism followed the crisis of the 17th century
The estates society is the background of court society

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern Kl. 7 (LB 6), Berlin/Brandenburg Kl. 7/8; NRW's Kernlehrplan G9 no longer lists absolutism as an obligatory focus.

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Enlightenment
topics.description: Pupils explain key ideas of the Enlightenment – reason, natural rights, social contract (Locke), separation of powers (Montesquieu), Kant's "sapere aude" – and how they challenged the estates society and absolutism.
evidence: Explains Kant's definition of Enlightenment in their own words
Explains the separation of powers according to Montesquieu
Explains why Enlightenment ideas threatened absolute monarchy
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard "Have the courage to use your own understanding", could they explain who said it and why it was revolutionary in the 18th century?

prerequisites.reason: Enlightenment thought criticised absolutist rule
Humanism and science prepared the new thinking

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The American Revolution
topics.description: Pupils explain why the thirteen colonies broke away from Britain ("no taxation without representation"), the Declaration of Independence (1776) and the US constitution, and ask who was excluded (enslaved people, women, Native Americans).
evidence: Explains the causes of the conflict between Britain and its colonies
Names the core principles of the Declaration of Independence
Contrasts the claim of equality with the reality of slavery
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read "all men are created equal" from 1776, could they explain what it meant then and whom it left out?

prerequisites.reason: The Declaration applies Enlightenment ideas

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats 1776 in the Kl. 9 longitudinal unit on human rights; NRW's Sek I plan leaves it out and covers it in the Einführungsphase (Kl. 11).

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The French Revolution
topics.description: Pupils distinguish the occasion (state bankruptcy, Estates-General) from the deeper causes of the French Revolution and outline its phases: National Assembly and storming of the Bastille, constitutional monarchy of 1791, Jacobin terror and Directory.
evidence: Distinguishes the occasion from the long-term causes of the revolution
Places the main phases from 1789 to 1799 on a timeline
Judges the actions of revolutionaries using the categories freedom and equality
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why the storming of the Bastille happened in 1789 and not earlier, could they separate the trigger from the deeper causes?

prerequisites.reason: Revolutionaries invoked Enlightenment ideas
The crisis of the estates society is a cause
The revolution overthrew an absolute monarchy

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Rights of Man of 1789
topics.description: Pupils analyse the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen and evaluate claim and reality: Olympe de Gouges' rights of women, slavery and the Haitian Revolution, and restrictions of rights during the Terror.
evidence: Names the core rights proclaimed in 1789
Explains Olympe de Gouges' criticism
Evaluates the gap between proclaimed rights and their implementation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared the 1789 Declaration with Olympe de Gouges' declaration of the rights of woman, could they explain what she criticised?

prerequisites.reason: The declaration is a product of the revolution
Links to basic rights in today's constitution

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Napoleon and Germany
topics.nameDe: Napoleon und das Ende des Alten Reiches
topics.description: Pupils explain how Napoleon reshaped Germany: secularisation and mediatisation (1803), the Confederation of the Rhine, the end of the Holy Roman Empire (1806), the Code civil, Prussian and Bavarian reforms, and the wars of liberation.
evidence: Explains why the Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806
Names reforms modelled on or provoked by France (e.g. Code civil, Prussian reforms, Montgelas)
Explains how resistance to Napoleon fostered German nationalism
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learned that their town became part of Bavaria or Württemberg around 1806, could they explain how Napoleon caused this?

prerequisites.reason: Napoleon rose from the revolution
The old territorial order was swept away

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Congress of Vienna and Restoration
topics.nameDe: Wiener Kongress, Deutscher Bund und Vormärz
topics.description: Pupils explain the new European order of 1815 (restoration, legitimacy, balance of power), the German Confederation, the suppression of liberal and national movements (Karlsbad Decrees) and the protests of the Vormärz (Wartburg, Hambach).
evidence: Names the principles and results of the Congress of Vienna
Explains the aims of the liberal and national movements
Explains the colours black-red-gold as a symbol of the Hambach Festival
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked where the German flag's colours come from, could they connect them with the national and liberal movement after 1815?

prerequisites.reason: The Congress reordered Europe after Napoleon

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Revolution of 1848/49
topics.nameDe: Die Revolution von 1848/49 und die Paulskirche
topics.description: Pupils describe the March Revolution, the Frankfurt National Assembly in the Paulskirche, its constitution and basic rights, the debate over "kleindeutsch" or "großdeutsch", and judge why the revolution failed.
evidence: Describes the goals of the revolutionaries of 1848
Explains the choice between a smaller and a greater German solution
Judges the reasons for the failure of the revolution
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visited the Paulskirche in Frankfurt, could they explain what happened there in 1848/49 and why it still matters for German democracy?

prerequisites.reason: The revolution grew out of the Vormärz
The Paulskirche basic rights build on the ideas of 1789

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Industrial Revolution
topics.description: Pupils explain why industrialisation began in Britain (steam engine, textiles, coal) and how Germany caught up after 1834–50 (Zollverein, railways, coal and steel in the Ruhr), distinguishing phases and regional differences.
evidence: Names preconditions of industrialisation in Britain
Explains the role of the railways and the Zollverein in Germany's "take-off"
Describes regional differences of industrial development in Germany
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a map of the German railway network in 1850 and 1880, could they explain how railways drove industrialisation?

prerequisites.reason: The Ruhr's rise was met in Erdkunde Kl. 6
Steam engines convert heat into motion

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Social Question
topics.description: Pupils describe working and living conditions of men, women and children in factories and growing cities – long hours, child labour, poor housing, no social security – that made up the "social question".
evidence: Describes a worker family's day using sources
Explains why child labour was widespread
Compares living conditions in the countryside and the industrial city
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read a factory regulation from 1850, could they describe what working life was like and why people called it the social question?

prerequisites.reason: The social question results from industrialisation

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Answers to the Social Question
topics.description: Pupils compare answers to the social question: trade unions and the SPD, Marx's theory of class struggle, church welfare (Kolping, Ketteler), entrepreneurs' welfare schemes (Krupp) and Bismarck's social insurance laws (1883–89).
evidence: Compares the solutions offered by workers' movement, churches, entrepreneurs and the state
Explains Marx's idea of class struggle in simple terms
Explains why Bismarck introduced social insurance alongside the anti-socialist laws
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learned that Germany's health insurance dates from 1883, could they explain why Bismarck introduced it?

prerequisites.reason: The answers respond to the social question

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Founding of the German Empire
topics.description: Pupils explain how Prussia under Bismarck unified Germany "from above" through three wars (1864, 1866, 1870/71), the proclamation in Versailles, and what the Franco-Prussian War meant for national self-image and Franco-German relations.
evidence: Describes the three wars of unification and their results
Analyses the painting of the proclamation in Versailles as a source
Explains why unification "from above" differed from the goals of 1848
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at Anton von Werner's painting of the proclamation of the Kaiser in 1871, could they explain who is shown and what it says about the new Reich?

prerequisites.reason: Contrasts unification from above with the failed attempt of 1848
Analysing a history painting

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Politics and Society in the Kaiserreich
topics.nameDe: Das Deutsche Kaiserreich: Verfassung und Gesellschaft
topics.description: Pupils describe the constitution of 1871 (Kaiser, chancellor, Reichstag with universal male suffrage), authoritarian and militarist attitudes, the fight against "enemies of the Reich" (Kulturkampf, anti-socialist laws), the women's movement, and judge the Empire between progress and backwardness.
evidence: Draws and explains a diagram of the 1871 constitution
Explains the Kulturkampf and the anti-socialist laws
Judges the Kaiserreich using examples of modernity and authoritarianism
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard the story of the "Hauptmann von Köpenick", could they explain what it says about the role of the military in Wilhelmine society?

prerequisites.reason: The Kaiserreich was founded in 1871
The SPD and social laws are part of domestic politics

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Imperialism in Africa
topics.description: Pupils explain economic, political, ideological (racism, "civilising mission") and social motives of European imperialism, the "scramble for Africa" and the Berlin Conference (1884/85), and the consequences for colonised societies.
evidence: Names and illustrates the main motives of imperialism
Explains how the Berlin Conference divided Africa
Describes consequences of colonial rule for African societies
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a map of Africa in 1914, could they explain how almost the whole continent came under European rule?

prerequisites.reason: Colonial expansion began in the early modern period
Industrial needs for raw materials and markets drove imperialism

osMatches.note: os: causes of British colonies in Australia

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: German Colonialism and the Herero Genocide
topics.nameDe: Deutsche Kolonialherrschaft und der Völkermord an Herero und Nama
topics.description: Pupils describe German colonial rule in Africa and the Pacific and the war against the Herero and Nama in German South West Africa (1904–08), recognised by Germany as genocide in 2021, and evaluate how this history is remembered (street names, restitution).
evidence: Locates the German colonies on a map
Describes the course and character of the war against the Herero and Nama
Evaluates a local example of colonial memory such as a street name
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard a debate about renaming a street named after a colonial officer, could they explain the history behind it?

prerequisites.reason: German colonialism is part of European imperialism

osMatches.note: os: impact of colonies on First Nations Australians

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Road to the First World War
topics.nameDe: Der Weg in den Ersten Weltkrieg: Bündnisse und Julikrise
topics.description: Pupils distinguish the occasion (Sarajevo assassination, 28 June 1914) from the causes of the First World War (alliances, arms race, nationalism, imperial rivalry) and judge the decisions of politicians in the July Crisis.
evidence: Draws the alliance systems of 1914
Separates the occasion from long-term causes
Judges the "blank cheque" and other decisions of the July Crisis
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether the shot in Sarajevo caused the First World War, could they explain the difference between trigger and causes?

prerequisites.reason: Imperial rivalry is a cause of the war
Distinguishing occasion and causes was first practised for 1789

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The First World War as Modern War
topics.nameDe: Der Erste Weltkrieg als moderner Krieg
topics.description: Pupils explain what made the First World War a new kind of war: trench warfare and battles of attrition (Verdun), new weapons (gas, machine guns, tanks), propaganda and the home front with hunger and women's work.
evidence: Describes trench warfare using soldiers' letters or photos
Explains the term "Materialschlacht" using Verdun
Describes changes on the home front
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read a soldier's letter from Verdun, could they explain why this war was so different from earlier ones?

prerequisites.reason: Follows the outbreak of the war
Industrial production made mass warfare possible

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: 1917: A Turning Point
topics.description: Pupils explain why 1917 is called a turning point: the USA entered the war and the Russian revolutions brought the Bolsheviks to power, creating two new world-political models (Wilson's liberal democracy and Lenin's communism).
evidence: Explains why the USA entered the war
Describes the February and October revolutions in Russia
Discusses why 1917 can be seen as the start of a new era
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why some historians start the "short 20th century" in 1917, could they explain the two events behind this?

prerequisites.reason: 1917 is a turning point within the war

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Paris Peace Treaties
topics.description: Pupils describe the end of the war (armistice of November 1918), Wilson's Fourteen Points and the Treaty of Versailles (territories, reparations, war-guilt article 231), and explain the different views of it in Germany and among the victors.
evidence: Names the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles
Compares German and French views of the treaty
Explains the idea of the League of Nations
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a German poster against the "Diktat von Versailles", could they explain the terms of the treaty and why many Germans rejected it?

prerequisites.reason: Wilson's ideas shaped the peace
The treaty ended the war

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The November Revolution 1918/19
topics.description: Pupils explain how the monarchy ended in November 1918 and the choice between a council system and a parliamentary democracy, the Spartacist uprising and the elections to the National Assembly in January 1919 (first vote for women).
evidence: Describes the events from the sailors' revolt to the proclamation of the republic
Compares council democracy and parliamentary democracy
Explains the significance of women's suffrage in 1919
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learned that the republic was proclaimed twice on 9 November 1918, could they explain the two different visions behind this?

prerequisites.reason: The revolution and the end of the war belong together
The revolution overthrew the imperial order

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Weimar Constitution
topics.description: Pupils analyse the Weimar Constitution – Reichstag elected by pure proportional representation, strong Reich President with emergency powers (Art. 48), basic rights, referendums – and explain its strengths and weaknesses.
evidence: Draws and explains a diagram of the Weimar Constitution
Explains the role of Article 48
Compares the constitution with that of 1871
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a diagram of the Weimar Constitution, could they point to the features that later helped to undermine democracy?

prerequisites.reason: The constitution was drafted by the National Assembly of 1919
Comparison with the 1871 constitution

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Crisis and Stabilisation 1919–1929
topics.description: Pupils describe the crisis years up to 1923 (Kapp Putsch, political murders, occupation of the Ruhr, hyperinflation, Hitler Putsch), the stabilisation under Stresemann (Rentenmark, Dawes Plan, Locarno) and the cultural boom of mass media, consumer society and modern art.
evidence: Explains causes and consequences of the 1923 hyperinflation
Names elements of stabilisation under Stresemann
Describes new mass media and culture of the 1920s
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a banknote for one billion marks from 1923, could they explain how this happened and how the currency was stabilised?

prerequisites.reason: The young republic's institutions faced the crises
Reparations were a burden

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Great Depression and the End of Weimar
topics.description: Pupils explain the effects of the Great Depression (unemployment, radicalisation), the presidential cabinets from 1930, the rise of the NSDAP and the appointment of Hitler on 30 January 1933, and judge the responsibility of actors.
evidence: Relates unemployment figures to election results of 1928–1933
Explains how the presidential cabinets hollowed out parliamentary democracy
Judges the roles of Hindenburg, conservative elites and voters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared a chart of unemployment with NSDAP election results from 1928 to 1932, could they explain the connection and its limits?

prerequisites.reason: Ends the period of stabilisation
Art. 48 enabled the presidential cabinets

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Nazi Ideology

Explains the terms Volksgemeinschaft and Führerprinzip
Traces antisemitism back to older roots
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read a passage from a Nazi schoolbook, could they identify the ideological ideas in it and explain why they are false and dangerous?

Older forms of hostility towards Jews

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Nazi Seizure of Power 1933/34
topics.description: Pupils describe how the Nazis destroyed the constitutional state within months: Reichstag Fire Decree, Enabling Act, ban of parties and unions, Gleichschaltung of the Länder and society, the "Röhm Putsch" and Hitler as "Führer" in 1934.
evidence: Puts the steps from January 1933 to August 1934 in order
Explains the significance of the Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act
Explains the term Gleichschaltung with examples
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked how Hitler could become dictator "legally", could they explain the steps of 1933/34?

prerequisites.reason: The seizure of power follows the end of Weimar
The Weimar constitution was hollowed out

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Everyday Life in the Nazi State
topics.nameDe: Alltag zwischen Zustimmung, Propaganda und Terror
topics.description: Pupils describe life in the Nazi state between consent and repression: propaganda, Hitler Youth and BDM, the "Volksgemeinschaft" and its exclusions, terror by SS and Gestapo, and discuss the room for action of ordinary people.
evidence: Analyses a Nazi propaganda poster
Describes the aims of the Hitler Youth
Discusses the room for action of ordinary people in the dictatorship
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard a grandparent say that "not everything was bad" under Hitler, could they explain how propaganda and terror worked together?

Propaganda posters are analysed as images

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Persecution and Exclusion 1933–1939
topics.description: Pupils describe the step-by-step persecution of Jews (boycott 1933, Nuremberg Laws 1935, November Pogrom 1938) and of other groups (political opponents, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, Jehovah's Witnesses, people with disabilities) before the war.
evidence: Puts anti-Jewish measures of 1933–1939 in chronological order
Explains the Nuremberg Laws and their consequences
Describes the November Pogrom using a local example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learned that the synagogue in their town was destroyed on 9/10 November 1938, could they place this in the persecution of Jews since 1933?

prerequisites.reason: Persecution put ideology into practice
The dictatorship removed legal protection

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Nazi Foreign Policy and the Road to War
topics.nameDe: NS-Außenpolitik und Weg in den Krieg
topics.description: Pupils explain Nazi foreign policy from revision of Versailles to expansion: rearmament, Rhineland, "Anschluss" of Austria, Munich Agreement and appeasement, Hitler–Stalin Pact and the attack on Poland on 1 September 1939.
evidence: Puts the steps of Nazi foreign policy 1933–1939 in order
Explains the policy of appeasement
Judges the role of foreign-policy successes for consent to the regime
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why Britain and France gave in to Hitler in Munich in 1938, could they explain the policy of appeasement?

prerequisites.reason: Revision of Versailles was a central aim
"Lebensraum" ideology aimed at expansion

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Second World War
topics.nameDe: Der Zweite Weltkrieg in Europa und Asien
topics.description: Pupils outline the course of the Second World War: Blitzkrieg, war against the Soviet Union, the war in the Pacific after Pearl Harbor, the turning points (Stalingrad, D-Day), bombing war and the end in May and August 1945.
evidence: Places the main phases of the war on a timeline and map
Explains the global dimension including the Pacific war
Describes the end of the war in Europe and Asia
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a world map of 1942, could they explain how the war had become a world war?

prerequisites.reason: The war began with the attack on Poland

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The War of Annihilation in the East
topics.nameDe: Vernichtungskrieg und Verbrechen an der Zivilbevölkerung
topics.description: Pupils explain why the war against Poland and the Soviet Union was a racist war of annihilation: occupation crimes, starvation of prisoners of war, forced labour and the Wehrmacht's involvement in crimes.
evidence: Explains the difference between a conventional war and a war of annihilation
Describes crimes against civilians and prisoners of war
Explains the system of forced labour in Germany
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard someone claim that the Wehrmacht only fought a normal war, could they explain with evidence why historians disagree?

prerequisites.reason: The war of annihilation is part of the Second World War
Racism and "Lebensraum" ideology

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Holocaust
topics.description: Pupils describe the systematic murder of six million European Jews: ghettos, mass shootings by Einsatzgruppen, the Wannsee Conference and the extermination camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau, as well as the genocide of Sinti and Roma (Porajmos) and the "euthanasia" murders.
evidence: Describes the stages from persecution to systematic mass murder
Explains the role of the Wannsee Conference
Explains with a biography or testimony what the Holocaust meant for victims
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read the diary of Anne Frank or a survivor's testimony, could they place it in the history of the Holocaust?

prerequisites.reason: The Holocaust radicalised earlier persecution
Mass murder was linked to the war in the East

externalPrerequisites.subject: Religion & Ethik
externalPrerequisites.reason: Understanding the victims' religious and cultural life

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Resistance against National Socialism
topics.description: Pupils describe forms of resistance – from non-conformity and help for persecuted people to the White Rose, Georg Elser, communist and church resistance and the attempt of 20 July 1944 – and judge motives and room for action.
evidence: Distinguishes forms of resistance from non-conformity to assassination attempts
Describes the White Rose or 20 July 1944 using sources
Judges motives and risks of resistance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read a leaflet of the White Rose, could they explain the students' motives and the risk they took?

prerequisites.reason: Resistance is set against consent and terror

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Flight and Expulsion 1944–1950
topics.nameDe: Flucht und Vertreibung im europäischen Kontext
topics.description: Pupils explain the flight and expulsion of Germans from the eastern territories and Eastern Europe at the end of the war and after, place it in the context of Nazi expansion and population policy, and assess its consequences for the victims and post-war society.
evidence: Explains causes of flight and expulsion in the context of Nazi crimes and war
Describes the experience of refugees using eyewitness accounts
Assesses the integration of expellees in post-war Germany
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learned that a great-grandparent came from Silesia after 1945, could they explain why millions of Germans had to leave their homes?

prerequisites.reason: Flight and expulsion followed the war

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: From Occupation to Two German States
topics.description: Pupils explain the Potsdam Conference (four zones, denazification, demilitarisation), the Nuremberg trials, the different developments in the zones, the currency reform and Berlin Blockade (1948/49) and the founding of the FRG and GDR in 1949.
evidence: Names the decisions of the Potsdam Conference
Explains how currency reform and Berlin Blockade deepened the division
Compares the founding of the FRG and the GDR
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why there were two German states from 1949, could they explain the steps from the four zones to the division?

prerequisites.reason: The occupation followed Germany's defeat
The Grundgesetz of 1949 was met in Kl. 6

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Cold War and Bloc Formation
topics.description: Pupils explain the ideological opposition of the USA and the USSR, containment (Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan), the formation of NATO and the Warsaw Pact, and how both German states were integrated into the blocs.
evidence: Compares the political and economic systems of the two superpowers
Explains the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan
Explains how rearmament and alliances gave both German states more sovereignty
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a map of Europe in 1955, could they explain why it was divided into two blocs?

prerequisites.reason: The opposition of liberal democracy and communism goes back to 1917
The division of Germany was part of bloc formation

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Cold War Crises and Proxy Wars
topics.nameDe: Krisen und Stellvertreterkriege: Korea, Kuba, Vietnam
topics.description: Pupils describe the Cold War in crises and proxy wars – Korea, the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, Vietnam – and explain nuclear deterrence, the arms race and détente.
evidence: Explains the term proxy war with an example
Describes the Cuban Missile Crisis and why it ended peacefully
Explains deterrence and the logic of the arms race
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that the world was close to nuclear war in October 1962, could they explain what happened in the Cuban Missile Crisis?

prerequisites.reason: Crises and proxy wars are part of the Cold War

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Decolonisation
topics.description: Pupils explain how colonies gained independence after 1945 (e.g. India 1947, Algeria 1962, Ghana 1957), distinguish peaceful and violent paths and short- and long-term consequences of post-colonial conflicts.
evidence: Explains why colonial empires collapsed after 1945
Compares a peaceful and a violent path to independence
Distinguishes short- and long-term consequences of decolonisation in one example
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared India's and Algeria's paths to independence, could they explain why one was largely non-violent and the other a war?

prerequisites.reason: Decolonisation ended the colonial empires

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: West Germany in the Adenauer Era
topics.nameDe: Die Bundesrepublik in der Ära Adenauer
topics.description: Pupils describe the early Federal Republic: integration into the West and reconciliation with France (Élysée Treaty 1963), the "economic miracle" and the social market economy, integration of expellees, recruitment of guest workers and the (often silent) handling of the Nazi past.
evidence: Explains Adenauer's policy of Western integration
Explains causes of the economic miracle
Describes how the Nazi past was dealt with in the 1950s
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watched a 1950s newsreel about the economic miracle, could they explain why West Germany grew so quickly and what was left out?

prerequisites.reason: The FRG was founded in 1949
Western integration took place in the Cold War

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The GDR as SED Dictatorship
topics.description: Pupils describe state and society in the GDR: the SED's claim to leadership, the Stasi, planned economy, youth organisations (FDJ), the uprising of 17 June 1953, everyday life, opposition and church groups.
evidence: Explains the SED's claim to power and the role of the Stasi
Describes the uprising of 17 June 1953
Compares everyday life in the GDR with life in the FRG
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visited the former Stasi prison in Berlin-Hohenschönhausen, could they explain how the SED kept control over society?

prerequisites.reason: The GDR was founded in 1949

topics.laenderNotes: Taught in more depth in the eastern Länder; Berlin/Brandenburg and Sachsen add regional studies of everyday life in the GDR.

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Berlin Wall and Ostpolitik
topics.description: Pupils explain why the GDR built the Berlin Wall in 1961, what it meant for people, and how relations between the two states changed through Brandt's new Ostpolitik (Basic Treaty 1972) and détente.
evidence: Explains the reasons for building the Wall from the GDR's point of view and its consequences
Explains the idea of "Wandel durch Annäherung"
Judges the room for action of politicians in both states
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} stood at the Berlin Wall memorial on Bernauer Straße, could they explain why the Wall was built and how relations changed in the 1970s?

prerequisites.reason: The Wall was built by the GDR
Contrasts with Adenauer's policy of strength

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: The Peaceful Revolution of 1989
topics.description: Pupils explain the causes of the collapse of the GDR – economic crisis, Gorbachev's reforms, opening of the Hungarian border, mass flight, the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig – and the fall of the Wall on 9 November 1989.
evidence: Distinguishes long-term causes from immediate triggers of 1989
Explains the role of Gorbachev and of the Eastern European reform movements
Describes the Monday demonstrations and the fall of the Wall
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard the chant "Wir sind das Volk", could they explain where and why it was shouted in autumn 1989?

prerequisites.reason: Follows German-German relations
The revolution ended the SED dictatorship

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: German Reunification 1990
topics.description: Pupils describe the steps to unity in 1990 – free Volkskammer election, monetary union, Two-plus-Four Treaty, unification on 3 October – and judge the economic and social transformation in the east (Treuhand, unemployment).
evidence: Places the steps to unity in 1990 in order
Explains why the Two-plus-Four Treaty was needed
Judges economic and social consequences of unification
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why 3 October is a public holiday, could they explain the steps that led to German unity in 1990?

prerequisites.reason: Reunification followed the fall of the Wall
The end of the Cold War made unity possible

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Source Criticism
topics.description: Students interpret sources of different genres in exam form: external and internal source criticism, analysis of argument and language, contextualisation and judgement of the source's value for a question, including digital and AI-generated material.
evidence: Writes a full source interpretation with description, analysis, context and judgement
Judges the value of a source genre for a given question
Checks a digital or AI-generated text for authenticity and plausibility
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were given an unknown speech from 1933 in an exam, could they write a structured interpretation that judges its reliability and value?

prerequisites.reason: Deepens the Sek I steps of interpretation
Judging perspective is part of criticism

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.reason: Analysing argument and rhetoric of a source

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Forming a Historical Judgement
topics.description: Students form reasoned judgements on historical questions, weighting several categories (e.g. continuity and change, freedom, power) and time levels, check whether their information is sufficient, and revise hypotheses in the light of evidence.
evidence: Uses explicit criteria and categories in a written judgement
Distinguishes judging by the standards of the time and by present-day norms
Checks and revises a hypothesis against new evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked "Was the revolution of 1848 a failure?", could they write a judgement that names its criteria and weighs arguments on both sides?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on factual and value judgements
Judgements weigh different perspectives

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Discussing Historians' Interpretations
topics.description: Students analyse and discuss interpretations from historiography – e.g. the Fischer controversy on war guilt, the "Sonderweg" thesis or debates on the end of Weimar – identifying the thesis, arguments and position of the historian.
evidence: Identifies thesis, arguments and evidence in a historian's text
Compares two conflicting interpretations of the same event
Discusses the plausibility of an interpretation with own knowledge
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read two historians disagreeing about who caused the First World War, could they lay out both positions and argue which is more convincing?

prerequisites.reason: Analysing accounts uses the tools of source criticism
Accounts as interpretations were met in Sek I

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: How Historical Knowledge Is Made
topics.description: Students reflect on the nature of historical knowledge: history as a reconstruction from sources, the perspective and present-day questions of historians, objectivity and plausibility, and the meaning of historical concepts and narrative.
evidence: Explains why history is a reconstruction rather than the past itself
Explains criteria of plausibility (empirical, normative, narrative)
Reflects on how present-day questions shape historical research
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether history can ever be objective, could they give a reasoned answer that explains how historians work?

prerequisites.reason: Controversies show the constructed nature of history
Judgement criteria are reflected theoretically

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Coming to Terms with the Nazi Past
topics.nameDe: Vergangenheitsbewältigung und Erinnerungskultur in Ost und West
topics.description: Students evaluate how both German states and united Germany dealt with Nazi crimes: denazification, Nuremberg and Auschwitz trials, antifascism as state doctrine in the GDR, debates (Historikerstreit) and memorials such as the Holocaust Memorial in Berlin.
evidence: Compares the handling of the Nazi past in the FRG and the GDR
Explains the significance of the Frankfurt Auschwitz trials
Evaluates a current memorial or debate on remembrance
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} visited the Holocaust Memorial in Berlin, could they explain how German remembrance of the Nazi past developed after 1945?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on Sek I memorial culture
Remembrance refers to Nazi crimes
The 1950s handling of the past

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Nation, Nationalism and Empire
topics.nameDe: Nation, Nationalismus und Imperium als Begriffe
topics.description: Students define and distinguish key concepts – nation (state nation, cultural nation, "imagined community"), nationalism (liberal and integral) and empire – and apply them to examples from the 19th and 20th centuries.
evidence: Distinguishes state nation and cultural nation with examples
Distinguishes liberal-emancipatory from integral nationalism
Names characteristics of an empire and applies them to one case
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard Germany described as a "Kulturnation" before 1871, could they explain what this means and how it differs from France?

prerequisites.reason: The national movement after 1815
The German nation-state of 1871 is a key case

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Modernisation Processes
topics.description: Students explain indicators of social, economic and technological modernisation around 1900 (urbanisation, industry, science, mass society, democratisation) and judge the effects of industrialisation on living conditions under social and ecological aspects, including ambivalent reactions to modernity.
evidence: Names and explains indicators of modernisation
Judges social and ecological effects of industrialisation
Explains ambivalent reactions to modernity (e.g. life reform, cultural pessimism)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared Berlin in 1850 and 1910, could they explain what "modernisation" means using concrete indicators?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on Sek I industrialisation
The Kaiserreich between progress and stagnation

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: German Jews and Modern Antisemitism
topics.description: Students describe emancipation and social integration of German Jews in the 19th century, the rise of racial antisemitism in the Kaiserreich and Weimar, and how Jewish families reacted to exclusion.
evidence: Describes steps of Jewish emancipation in the 19th century
Explains the difference between religious anti-Judaism and racial antisemitism
Describes reactions of German-Jewish families to exclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read about a Jewish family that fought for Germany in 1914 and was persecuted after 1933, could they explain this history of integration and exclusion?

prerequisites.reason: Older forms of hostility towards Jews
Nazi antisemitism radicalised earlier ideas
Antisemitism as reaction to modernity

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Participation and Freedom: A Longitudinal Study
topics.nameDe: Politische Partizipation und Freiheitsstreben im Längsschnitt
topics.description: Students compare struggles for participation and freedom across epochs – Athenian democracy, conflicts in late-medieval towns, the American and French revolutions with their debates on slavery, and 1848/49 – asking who could take part and where the limits lay.
evidence: Compares participation in Athens and in a late-medieval town
Explains the contemporary debates about slavery and abolitionism
Discusses the aims and options of the groups in 1848/49
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked who could take part in politics in Athens, in a medieval town and in 1848, could they compare the three and name the excluded?

prerequisites.reason: Athenian democracy was introduced in Kl. 6
The revolutions are revisited in depth
1848/49 is revisited

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Explaining National Socialism
topics.description: Students discuss different explanations of National Socialism – intentionalist and structuralist views, polycracy, "Sonderweg", totalitarianism and fascism theories, consent and "Volksgemeinschaft" – and judge their explanatory power.
evidence: Explains two contrasting explanations of the Nazi dictatorship
Explains the intentionalism–functionalism debate on the Holocaust
Judges the explanatory power and limits of one approach
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked whether the Nazi regime was run by Hitler alone, could they compare explanations that stress Hitler and those that stress structures?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on Sek I knowledge of the dictatorship
Discussing historians' interpretations

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Comparing Twentieth-Century Dictatorships
topics.description: Students compare National Socialism and Stalinism (and optionally the SED state) using totalitarianism theory (Arendt, Friedrich/Brzezinski), discuss its strengths and the criticism of it, and reflect on comparing without equating.
evidence: Names criteria of totalitarian rule according to a theory
Compares Nazi and Stalinist rule using these criteria
Discusses criticism of the totalitarianism concept
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard the claim "Hitler and Stalin were the same", could they compare the two regimes carefully and show where the comparison works and where it fails?

prerequisites.reason: Totalitarianism is one of the explanatory approaches
Stalinism is studied in the E-Phase

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: China and Russia as Empires
topics.description: Students characterise the imperial foundations of China and Russia around 1900, explain the revolutionary upheavals (China 1911 and 1949, Russia 1917), judge Maoism and Stalinism, and assess the reforms of Deng Xiaoping and Gorbachev and imperial self-images ("Middle Kingdom", "russkij mir").
evidence: Describes the imperial structures of China and Russia around 1900
Explains the consequences of the revolutions of 1917 and 1949
Judges the reform policies of Deng Xiaoping and Gorbachev
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard Russian politicians speak of the "Russian world", could they explain the imperial history behind this idea?

prerequisites.reason: The Russian revolution was introduced in Sek I
Uses the concept of empire

topics.laenderNotes: NRW (from 2027) makes China and Russia obligatory in the Einführungsphase; BW offers Russia and China as electives in Kl. 9/10.

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Colonialism and Its Legacies
topics.nameDe: Kolonialismus und seine Folgen für die globalisierte Welt
topics.description: Students explain motives and forms of European colonialism and its effects on today's world – borders, economic structures, racism, migration – and evaluate how Germany remembers its colonial history (restitution of artefacts, recognition of genocide).
evidence: Explains forms of colonial rule (settler, trade and exploitation colonies)
Traces present-day problems of a post-colonial region back to colonial rule
Evaluates a current debate on colonial remembrance in Germany
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard about the return of the Benin Bronzes to Nigeria, could they explain the colonial history behind the debate?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on Sek I German colonial history
Decolonisation was introduced in Sek I

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: Decolonisation: Case Study Namibia
topics.description: Students evaluate a decolonisation process in depth – e.g. Namibia's path from German colony to South African rule, apartheid and independence in 1990 – and the role of non-aligned states and the UN.
evidence: Describes the stages of Namibia's path to independence
Explains the role of the UN and the non-aligned movement
Evaluates the results of decolonisation and the German–Namibian reconciliation process
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} followed the German–Namibian negotiations about the genocide, could they explain Namibia's long road to independence?

prerequisites.reason: Deepens the study of colonialism
Builds on Sek I decolonisation

topics.subject: Geschichte
topics.name: After the Boom: 1973 and Structural Change
topics.nameDe: Nach dem Boom: Ölkrise 1973 und Strukturwandel
topics.description: Students explain the end of the post-war boom with the oil crisis of 1973, the "limits to growth" debate, structural change and unemployment in the West, the economic crisis in the GDR, and new social movements (environmental and peace movements).
evidence: Explains the causes and effects of the 1973 oil crisis
Compares economic developments in East and West Germany after 1973
Explains the rise of the environmental movement in the context of the growth debate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard about the car-free Sundays of 1973, could they explain why the oil crisis marked the end of the post-war boom?

prerequisites.reason: The boom years preceded the crisis
The GDR economy is compared

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Analysing Complex Thematic Maps
topics.description: Pupils analyse thematic maps with several layers of information (e.g. economic, population-density or climate maps in the atlas): they read the legend, describe distributions and patterns, and explain them with other knowledge.
evidence: Describes the spatial distribution shown on a thematic map from general to specific
Combines two thematic maps to explain a pattern
Names the limits of what a map shows (scale, date, generalisation)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were given an atlas map of Europe's agriculture, could they describe the pattern and explain it with climate and relief?

prerequisites.reason: Builds on reading physical and thematic maps
Uses the atlas index and grid

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Geographical Diagrams and Statistics
topics.nameDe: Diagramme und Statistiken auswerten und erstellen
topics.description: Pupils read and draw diagrams used in geography – line, bar and pie charts, combined climate charts, tables of indicators – choose the suitable diagram for data, and check axes, units and sources critically.
evidence: Chooses a suitable diagram type for a given data set
Draws a correct diagram with labelled axes, units and source
Spots a misleading axis or missing source in a diagram
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had a table of a country's population for 1950–2020, could they draw a suitable diagram and describe the trend?

prerequisites.reason: Pie charts and relative frequencies from Mathematik
Critical reading of data displays
Climate charts are a combined diagram

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Working with GIS and Web Maps
topics.nameDe: Mit WebGIS und digitalen Karten arbeiten
topics.description: Pupils use web-based geographic information systems and map services: switch and combine layers, measure distances and areas, query data, read satellite images and create a simple thematic map of their own.
evidence: Combines two data layers in a WebGIS to answer a question
Measures a distance or area and queries attribute data
Creates and exports a simple thematic map with legend
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} used a WebGIS to find flood-risk zones near their town, could they combine the layers and present the result as a map?

prerequisites.reason: GIS layers are thematic maps
Understanding data as stored information

topics.laenderNotes: GIS is obligatory in NRW (MK12) and BW (3.3.1.1 "Digitale Orientierung", Kl. 9/10); other Länder use it as a method without a fixed grade.

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Causal Diagrams of Geographical Systems
topics.description: Pupils represent geographical processes as causal diagrams (Wirkungsgefüge): they link causes and effects with arrows, mark feedback loops and use the diagram to explain processes such as desertification or rainforest clearing.
evidence: Draws a causal diagram with at least five linked factors
Marks a reinforcing feedback loop and explains it
Uses a diagram to explain a process in writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked how overgrazing leads to desertification, could they draw a causal diagram showing the chain and the feedback loop?

prerequisites.reason: Representing information graphically
Landscape zones show how factors interact

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Material-Based Regional Analysis
topics.description: Students carry out a question-led analysis of a region using several materials (maps, statistics, diagrams, texts, images) as in the Abitur exam: they apply operators, link the materials, cite them correctly and reach a reasoned judgement.
evidence: Structures an analysis according to the operators of the three requirement levels
Links information from at least four materials with correct references
Formulates a reasoned judgement on a spatial problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} received an Abitur-style task with eight materials on a region in Brazil, could they write a structured analysis that links the materials and ends with a judgement?

prerequisites.reason: Map analysis is one part
Diagram analysis is one part
Linking factors into a system

externalPrerequisites.subject: Deutsch
externalPrerequisites.concept: analysing non-continuous texts and writing a structured analysis

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Earth's Structure and Plate Tectonics
topics.description: Pupils describe the Earth's layers (crust, mantle, core) and explain plate tectonics: convection in the mantle, divergent and convergent plate boundaries, subduction and transform faults, with examples such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the Andes.
evidence: Labels a cross-section of the Earth's layers
Explains plate movement with convection currents
Distinguishes divergent, convergent and transform boundaries with examples
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a world map of plate boundaries, could they explain why Iceland is splitting apart and the Andes are rising?

prerequisites.reason: Uses the world map of continents and oceans
Mountain building was met with the Alps

topics.laenderNotes: Bayern treats volcanism and earthquakes with the physical geography of Europe in Kl. 7; NRW places plate tectonics in its Kl. 7–10 block (IF 4, usually Kl. 7/8); BW (G8) puts endogenous processes in Kl. 9/10.

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Volcanoes
topics.description: Pupils explain how volcanoes form at plate boundaries and hotspots, distinguish shield and stratovolcanoes by magma type and eruption, and describe hazards and benefits (fertile soils, geothermal energy, tourism) of volcanic regions.
evidence: Explains why most volcanoes lie at plate boundaries
Compares a shield volcano and a stratovolcano
Names benefits and dangers of living near a volcano
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared Etna and a Hawaiian volcano, could they explain why they erupt so differently?

prerequisites.reason: Volcanism is explained by plate tectonics

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Earthquakes and Tsunamis
topics.description: Pupils explain how earthquakes arise from stress at plate boundaries, how their strength is measured (magnitude) and how seaquakes trigger tsunamis, using a recent example.
evidence: Explains the origin of an earthquake with focus and epicentre
Explains magnitude and why damage also depends on building quality
Describes how a tsunami forms and spreads
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} read about the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake, could they explain how it caused the tsunami?

prerequisites.reason: Earthquakes are explained by plate movement

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Living in Hazard Zones
topics.description: Pupils explain why people live and work in tectonically active areas despite the risks (soils, raw materials, energy, tourism), and discuss measures of disaster prevention such as early warning, earthquake-proof building and evacuation plans.
evidence: Explains why people settle in hazard zones
Names and evaluates measures of disaster prevention
Judges how far a region is suitable for settlement
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why millions live around Naples near Vesuvius, could they weigh the benefits against the risks?

prerequisites.reason: Volcanic hazards
Earthquake hazards

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: The Earth System and Geofactors
topics.nameDe: Das System Erde: Geofaktoren und Geosphären
topics.description: Students describe the Earth as a system of interacting geofactors (relief, climate, water, soil, vegetation, humans) and spheres, and explain how landscapes result from their interaction and how human activity changes them.
evidence: Names the geofactors and explains their interaction in one landscape
Explains the human being as a geofactor with examples
Represents a landscape as a system with flows and feedbacks
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked why the Sahel looks the way it does, could they explain it as the interplay of climate, soil, vegetation and people?

prerequisites.reason: Systems are represented as causal diagrams
Landscape zones show the interaction of geofactors

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Natural Hazards, Risk and Vulnerability
topics.description: Students distinguish hazard, risk and disaster, explain the vulnerability of societies (poverty, building quality, governance) and evaluate disaster risk reduction at regional, national and global level, using earthquakes, volcanoes and tropical cyclones.
evidence: Explains why the same hazard causes very different damage in different countries
Explains the concept of vulnerability with indicators
Evaluates measures of disaster risk reduction
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compared the effects of similar earthquakes in Haiti and in Japan, could they explain the difference using the concept of vulnerability?

prerequisites.reason: Deepens Sek I knowledge of hazard zones
Development level shapes vulnerability

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Climate Zones of the Earth
topics.description: Pupils explain how the angle of the sun's rays creates temperature zones and describe the climate zones of the Earth (tropical, subtropical, temperate, subpolar, polar) using climate charts and a climate-zone map.

Assigns climate charts to the correct climate zone

Uses climate charts

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Global Circulation and the Trade Winds
topics.description: Pupils explain air pressure and wind, the trade-wind circulation with the Intertropical Convergence Zone and the seasonal shift of zenithal rains, and use it to explain rainy and dry seasons in the tropics.

Convection of warm air

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: The Greenhouse Effect

Primary-school introduction to climate change
Reading climate curves

externalPrerequisites.subject: Physik

externalPrerequisites.reason: Physical basis of the greenhouse effect

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Consequences of Climate Change

Coastal protection in Germany

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Mitigation and Adaptation
topics.description: Pupils distinguish climate protection (reducing emissions) from adaptation (dykes, heat plans, drought-resistant crops), evaluate measures from personal behaviour to international agreements (Paris 2015) and local adaptation to extreme weather.

Mitigation targets the causes

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Climate Change as a Global Challenge

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Landscape Zones of the Earth

Natural location factors of farming

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: The Tropical Rainforest Ecosystem

Food webs and decomposers

externalPrerequisites.concept: nutrient cycles and decomposers in ecosystems

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Rainforest Use and Destruction
topics.description: Pupils explain causes and consequences of rainforest clearing (soy, cattle, palm oil, timber, mining), compare shifting cultivation, plantations and agroforestry, and judge approaches to sustainable use.

Intensive versus sustainable farming

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Drylands, Oases and Irrigation
topics.description: Pupils describe the climate and adaptations of desert regions, explain oasis farming, nomadism and modern irrigation, and assess consequences such as falling groundwater and soil salinisation.

Water availability limits farming

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: The Sahel and Desertification

The savanna is a landscape zone

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Agriculture in a Globalised World
topics.nameDe: Landnutzungswandel und Agrarwirtschaft im Kontext der Globalisierung

Global value chains

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: The Global Water Cycle and Water Availability

Primary-school water protection
Rivers as part of the water cycle

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Water Scarcity and Water Conflicts

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Use and Protection of the Oceans

Explains overfishing and plastic pollution with data

Oceans in the water cycle

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Economic Sectors and Tertiarisation

Reading sector diagrams

topics.name: Changing Location Factors

Changing factors drove structural change in the Ruhr

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Long-Haul Tourism and Development
topics.nameDe: Ferntourismus: Chancen und Risiken für Entwicklungsräume

evidence: Names economic opportunities of tourism for a developing country
Explains risks such as leakage and environmental damage
Compares mass tourism with community-based tourism

topics.subject: Erdkunde

Evaluates the success of a regional development strategy

The Ruhr was the introductory case in Kl. 6

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Tourism Area Life Cycle

Reading tourism statistics

Urban functions

topics.subject: Erdkunde
topics.name: Urban Structure and Functions

Explains causes of change in inner cities
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} walked from the old town to the edge of their city, could they describe the functional zones they cross?

topics.name: Urbanisation and Megacities

Explains the growth of informal settlements

Migration drives urban growth

topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were asked how their city could cope better with heatwaves and heavy rain, could they evaluate concepts like the sponge city?
